corrections.text: The headline characterizes the surviving claims as "Sensory's Tying Claims." None of the three sources reporting on Judge Mehta's July 2026 ruling (Bloomberg Law x2, Law360) describe the surviving claims using the term "tying." That term appears only in Sensory's original, since-superseded April 2022 complaint (Count II, an illegal-tying theory) and in an April 2025 MLex report of Google arguing the opposite — that Sensory's complaint lacks a valid tying theory. The headline's framing is a plausible inference from the case's litigation history, not a fact stated by the sources describing what actually survived the ruling.

Two quotes presented in quotation marks are paraphrases, not verbatim source text. The article attributes to Law360 the quote "permitted Sensory Inc., a software developer, to advance antitrust allegations focused on voice assistant and related technology markets, but eliminated its broader claims concerning general search and advertising sectors"; Law360's actual text reads "Software developer Sensory can pursue antitrust claims alleging Google illegally maintains monopolies over voice assistant and similar technology markets, but not its broader claims involving the general search and advertising markets." Separately, the article quotes MLex as saying Sensory "possesses no search engine or search product of its own"; MLex's actual text reads Sensory "has no search engine or search product of its own."
